newsitem.title: UK: MGAM says IMRO funds probe to continue.
newsitem.headline: MGAM says IMRO funds probe to continue.

text.p: Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM) said on Wednesday it would continue to work with UK investments watchdog, the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation (IMRO) and other regulators in the investigations into irregularities in three of its funds.

"The initial internal investigation is largely complete and MGAM will continue to work with IMRO and other regulators to resolve outstanding issues," said Robert Smith, who has replaced Keith Percy as head of the troubled asset management arm.
Problems at the three unit trust investment funds emerged last month and led to the sacking of fund manager Peter Young.

Young was dismissed by Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, the investment banking arm of Germany's Deutsche Bank, for alleged "gross misconduct" following the discovery of misvaluations of speculative, unlisted stocks in two funds he managed.
He is currently being investigated by Britain's Serious Fraud Office (SFO) but has denied any criminal activity and said he is being made a scapegoat.

IMRO is conducting its own investigation into the funds but is not expected to report on its findings for some months. The findings could lead to hefty fines against MGAM and possible action against individuals.

Smith said the priority was to restore MGAM's reputation in the unit trust business and that if compensation was found to be due to investors under IMRO rules or other legislation, the group would pay it.

DMG said in a statement that four directors, Keith Percy, Glyn Owen, Graham Kane and Michael Wheatley were leaving MGAM under the terms of their contracts, along with a senior associate director Paul Ebling.

DMG chief executive Michael Dobson said they had made "a major contribution to our asset management business over many years", adding that Smith was the natural choice to take over as head of the business.
Smith said he was determined that MGAM would continue to deliver "superior performance for clients in virtually every asset class".
Deutsche had to make a 180 million stg cash injection to shore up the three funds, which were temporarily suspended early last month following the discovery of irregularities in them.
